title: Lec 07 — Cardiac Cellular Electrophysiology
subtitle: Week 02 · Lec 07 · Cardiac Cellular Electrophysiology | 18 questions

questions.text: A cardiomyocyte maintains a stable resting membrane potential of approximately −90 mV between beats. Which statement best explains why this value is close to the K+ equilibrium potential rather than the Na+ equilibrium potential?
options: Voltage-gated Na+ channels are maximally open at rest, driving Na+ influx that partially offsets K+ efflux and stabilizes the potential near −90 mV
Resting K+ conductance is high relative to Na+ conductance, so the membrane potential is pulled toward EK; the low resting Na+ permeability prevents a significant Na+ contribution
The Na+/K+-ATPase pump actively maintains −90 mV by pumping three Na+ out for every two K+ in, generating a dominant electrogenic potential

Resting Na+ conductance exceeds K+ conductance, but the large extracellular Na+ concentration gradient is offset by the small intracellular K+ gradient, producing a net inside-negative potential near −90 mV
questions.explanation:
At rest the membrane is much more permeable to K+ than to Na+, so K+ efflux dominates and the membrane potential is pulled close to EK (−90 mV). Low resting Na+ permeability means Na+ has almost no influence on resting potential despite its large driving force.
Option A is incorrect: voltage-gated Na+ channels are closed at rest; opening them would depolarize, not stabilize, the cell.
Option C is incorrect: the Na+/K+-ATPase contributes only a small electrogenic component; the dominant determinant is passive K+ conductance.
Option D is incorrect: resting Na+ conductance is far lower than K+ conductance; the premise is reversed.

questions.text: The intracellular K+ concentration of a ventricular myocyte is approximately 140 mM while extracellular K+ is approximately 4 mM. Which of the following is the direct consequence of this gradient for resting membrane potential?
options: K+ flows inward down its concentration gradient, building up positive charge inside and hyperpolarizing the cell to −90 mV

The K+ gradient is irrelevant to the resting membrane potential because the sarcolemma is impermeable to K+ at rest, and the potential is set entirely by the electrogenic activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump
K+ is distributed equally at equilibrium, so the gradient exerts no net force on K+ movement at the resting potential
K+ efflux down its concentration gradient creates net negative charge inside; this continues until the electrical force opposing efflux balances the chemical driving force, establishing EK ≈ −90 mV
questions.explanation:
With [K+]i = 140 mM and [K+]o = 4 mM, the chemical gradient strongly favors K+ efflux. K+ exits through background K+ channels until the inside-negative electrical potential is large enough to oppose further outflow, establishing EK ≈ −90 mV. The resting membrane potential sits near this value because resting K+ conductance is the dominant permeability.
Option A is incorrect: K+ flows outward (high to low concentration, 140 → 4), not inward.
Option B is incorrect: background K+ channels are open at rest, giving the membrane substantial K+ permeability.
Option C is incorrect: K+ is not in equal distribution; the 140/4 mM asymmetry is precisely what drives efflux and generates the resting potential.

questions.text: During Phase 0 of the ventricular action potential, voltage-gated Na+ channels open rapidly and drive the membrane potential toward +60 mV (ENa). At what point during Phase 0 do Na+ channels begin to inactivate?
options: Na+ channels begin to inactivate before the membrane potential reaches its peak, so depolarization stops short of the Na+ equilibrium potential
Na+ channels inactivate only after the membrane potential has reached and briefly sustained its peak at approximately +60 mV
Na+ channels remain open throughout Phase 0 and Phase 1, closing abruptly only when K+ efflux begins at the Phase 1 notch
Na+ channels do not inactivate during Phase 0; inactivation is triggered exclusively by the rise in intracellular Ca2+ during Phase 2, when L-type Ca2+ channels are open and slowly inactivating
questions.explanation:
The slide states explicitly: “Na+ channels start to inactivate before peak of cardiac action potential.” This early inactivation prevents the membrane from reaching ENa = +60 mV, which is why the actual peak is only around +30 mV.
Option B is incorrect: inactivation begins before the peak, not after it. The +60 mV value is never reached.
Option C is incorrect: Na+ channels begin inactivating well before Phase 1; their inactivation (along with Ito) defines Phase 1.
Option D is incorrect: inactivation is voltage-dependent, not Ca2+-triggered, and it begins during Phase 0 itself.

questions.text: During the Phase 2 plateau of the ventricular action potential, the membrane potential remains relatively stable for approximately 200 ms. Which combination of ionic events best accounts for this sustained plateau?
options: Voltage-gated Na+ channels are fully active and L-type Ca2+ channels are fully closed, so rapid Na+ influx alone sustains the plateau

IKr and IKs K+ channels are fully open and L-type Ca2+ channels have completely inactivated; the resulting unopposed outward K+ efflux gradually drives the membrane back toward −90 mV, effectively ending the plateau phase
Na+ channels are mostly inactivated but a small persistent Na+ current remains; L-type Ca2+ channels stay open while slowly inactivating, balancing the outward IKs and IKr K+ currents
The Na+/K+-ATPase runs at maximum speed during Phase 2, maintaining the plateau by re-establishing ion gradients in real time
questions.explanation:
During Phase 2: Na+ channels are mostly inactivated but a small persistent Na+ current continues; L-type Ca2+ channels are open and slowly inactivating; Ito has inactivated while IKs and IKr begin to open. The plateau represents a balance of these small inward currents against the growing outward K+ currents.
Option A is incorrect: Na+ channels are mostly inactivated by Phase 2, not fully active.
Option B is incorrect: IKr and IKs are only beginning to open (not fully open) at the start of Phase 2; that fully-open state characterizes Phase 3.
Option D is incorrect: the Na+/K+-ATPase is too slow to determine action potential shape on a millisecond timescale.

questions.text: At the transition from Phase 2 to Phase 3 (terminal repolarization), the membrane potential rapidly returns to −90 mV. Which ionic shift is most directly responsible for this rapid repolarization?
options: Voltage-gated Na+ channels reopen during Phase 3, driving a second inward current that overshoots −90 mV before rebounding
L-type Ca2+ channels fully inactivate and IKs and IKr K+ channels are maximally open; unopposed outward K+ current rapidly hyperpolarizes the cell back to −90 mV
The Na+/K+-ATPase accelerates during Phase 3, actively extruding Na+ to drive repolarization
Transient outward K+ channels (Ito) re-activate during Phase 3 and serve as the dominant repolarizing current driving the membrane back to −90 mV, independent of any contribution from IKr or IKs
questions.explanation:
In Phase 3: inward Ca2+ currents are fully inactivated and Ito remains inactivated, leaving only the fully-open IKs and IKr to drive outward K+ current. This unopposed efflux rapidly repolarizes the membrane back to the resting potential.
Option A is incorrect: Na+ channels are inactivated and do not reopen during Phase 3.
Option C is incorrect: the Na+/K+-ATPase acts over seconds, not on the millisecond timescale of Phase 3.
Option D is incorrect: Ito inactivated during Phase 1 and remains inactivated through Phase 3; it is not the dominant Phase 3 repolarizing current.

questions.text: Cardiac muscle, unlike skeletal muscle, cannot be tetanized (produce sustained fused contraction even with repeated rapid stimuli). What property of the cardiac action potential directly prevents tetany?
options: The absolute refractory period occupies most of the action potential duration, preventing re-excitation until relaxation is nearly complete
Cardiac myocytes lack the ryanodine receptor channels needed to sustain the elevated cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentration required to maintain the prolonged tetanic contraction seen in skeletal muscle
The Frank-Starling mechanism limits contractile force, preventing temporal summation of successive twitches needed for tetany
Slow conduction through the AV node introduces sufficient beat-to-beat delay to prevent temporal summation of contractions
questions.explanation:
The cardiac absolute refractory period lasts nearly as long as the contraction itself, so a second stimulus delivered during the twitch finds the cell non-excitable. This means the heart cannot be re-stimulated until it has already begun to relax — tetany is structurally impossible, protecting the heart’s pump function.
Option B is incorrect: cardiac myocytes do express ryanodine receptors (RyR2); they are essential for CICR and contraction.
Option C is incorrect: the Frank-Starling mechanism modulates stroke volume based on filling, not the timing of refractoriness.
Option D is incorrect: AV node delay sets beat rate but does not determine the cellular refractory period that prevents tetany.

questions.text: A premature stimulus is delivered to a ventricular myocyte during late Phase 3. The stimulus elicits an action potential with a slower-than-normal Phase 0 upstroke and reduced amplitude. Which period does this describe, and what is its ionic basis?
options: Absolute refractory period; voltage-gated Na+ channels have fully recovered from inactivation and are available but require an above-threshold stimulus to open

Absolute refractory period; no voltage-gated Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation, so even the strongest possible stimulus cannot generate a propagating action potential in the downstream myocardium
Relative refractory period; L-type Ca2+ channels are still fully open during late Phase 3, limiting the amplitude of the upstroke
Relative refractory period; only a fraction of Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation, so a stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed and the resulting upstroke is weaker than normal
questions.explanation:
An action potential that is elicited (evidence of excitability) but with reduced Vmax and amplitude defines the relative refractory period. During this period, some but not all Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation — enough to fire if the stimulus exceeds the threshold, but too few to produce a full-strength upstroke.
Option A is incorrect: if all Na+ channels have recovered, the upstroke would be normal in amplitude, not reduced.
Option B is incorrect: if no Na+ channels had recovered, no action potential could be generated at all — that is the absolute refractory period.
Option C is incorrect: L-type Ca2+ channel status does not determine the Phase 0 upstroke velocity in fast fibers; Na+ channel availability is the key variable.

questions.text: A drug reduces the number of available voltage-gated Na+ channels in ventricular myocytes. Tracing the downstream consequences, which sequence of effects best describes how this drug impairs ventricular pressure development?
options: Fewer Na+ channels → reduced K+ efflux during Phase 3 → prolonged action potential → increased L-type Ca2+ influx → exaggerated pressure development

Fewer Na+ channels → slowed gap-junction conduction → delayed electrical activation of the ventricle → delayed but ultimately normal peak pressure development, since downstream Ca2+ cycling is unaffected
Fewer Na+ channels → reduced Vmax of Phase 0 → reduced L-type Ca2+ influx during the plateau → reduced SR Ca2+ release (CICR) → decreased contractility → reduced dP/dt
Fewer Na+ channels → complete failure of Phase 0 → ventricular standstill with no pressure development at any dose; the effect is binary
questions.explanation:
Vmax is set by the number and gating rate of Na+ channels opening during Phase 0. Lower Vmax means a slower, less steep Phase 0, which reduces the speed and amplitude of L-type Ca2+ channel activation during the plateau, lowering CICR and contractility. The rate of ventricular pressure development (dP/dt) is therefore a downstream readout of Vmax.
Option A is incorrect: Na+ channel availability does not control K+ efflux during Phase 3; K+ efflux is driven by IKs and IKr.
Option B is incorrect: while slower conduction is a secondary consequence, the primary impairment of pressure development comes through the Vmax→Ca2+→CICR→dP/dt chain, not just delayed activation timing.
Option D is incorrect: reducing (not eliminating) Na+ channels proportionally reduces Vmax; the response is graded, not binary.

questions.text: A student states: “SA node action potentials are ‘slow’ because they last longer than ventricular action potentials.” A classmate corrects this. Which of the following is the accurate distinction between fast and slow cardiac action potentials?
options: “Fast” and “slow” refer to the rate of Phase 0 depolarization (Vmax), not to action potential duration; fast fibers use voltage-gated Na+ channels and have high Vmax, while slow fibers (SA/AV nodes) use L-type Ca2+ channels and have low Vmax

“Fast” and “slow” refer exclusively to action potential duration; fast fibers have characteristically short action potentials of approximately 50–100 ms, while slow fibers (SA/AV nodes) have much longer action potentials lasting 200–300 ms, accounting for the nodal delay
“Fast” fibers generate rapid ventricular pressure rise during systole, while “slow” fibers generate slow pressure rise; the terms describe mechanical speed, not electrical speed
“Fast” refers to recovery time after an action potential; fast fibers recover from inactivation faster because their action potentials are shorter, not because of Phase 0 velocity
questions.explanation:
The professor explicitly corrects this exact misconception: “fast action potentials is just because it depolarizes fast, not necessarily the time of action potential — it’s not a faster action potential duration.” Fast fibers (atrial/ventricular myocytes, His-Purkinje) have high Vmax because Phase 0 is driven by rapidly gating voltage-gated Na+ channels. Slow fibers (SA/AV nodes) have low Vmax because Phase 0 is driven by slowly gating L-type Ca2+ channels.
Option B is incorrect: the terms do not describe AP duration; both fast and slow fibers have prolonged plateaus (200–300 ms).
Option C is incorrect: the fast/slow terminology is purely about electrical Vmax, not mechanical pressure development speed.
Option D is incorrect: while recovery time does differ, that is a consequence of the gating kinetics difference, not the defining meaning of the terms.

questions.text: The electrical properties of fast cardiac fibers differ significantly from those of nodal (slow) fibers. Which set of values correctly describes a fast fiber (atrial/ventricular myocyte or His-Purkinje)?
options: AP amplitude 40–80 mV; AP threshold −45 mV; Vmax 1–10 V/s; conduction velocity 0.01–0.1 m/s; recovery time: slow
AP amplitude 40–80 mV; AP threshold −60 mV; Vmax 200–800 V/s; conduction velocity 0.5–3 m/s
AP amplitude 90–120 mV; AP threshold −45 mV; Vmax 1–10 V/s; conduction velocity 0.5–3 m/s
AP amplitude 90–120 mV; AP threshold −60 mV; Vmax 200–800 V/s; conduction velocity 0.5–3 m/s
questions.explanation:
From the comparison table: fast fibers have AP amplitude 90–120 mV, threshold −60 mV, Vmax 200–800 V/s, and conduction velocity 0.5–3 m/s. Slow fibers (SA/AV nodes) have amplitude 40–80 mV, threshold −45 mV, Vmax 1–10 V/s, and conduction velocity 0.01–0.1 m/s.
Option A is incorrect: amplitude 40–80 mV, threshold −45 mV, Vmax 1–10 V/s, and CV 0.01–0.1 m/s are all slow-fiber values.
Option B is incorrect: amplitude 40–80 mV is a slow-fiber value; the threshold and Vmax are mismatched across cell types.
Option C is incorrect: threshold −45 mV is a slow-fiber threshold and Vmax 1–10 V/s is a slow-fiber Vmax, despite the correct fast-fiber amplitude.

questions.text: The speed at which an action potential spreads through the myocardium depends on several variables. Which of the following correctly lists all four major determinants of myocardial conduction velocity as taught in this lecture?
options: Heart rate, action potential duration, extracellular Ca2+ concentration, and the length of gap junction channels
Current amplitude (number of open Na+ or Ca2+ channels), Vmax (rate of Phase 0 depolarization), threshold (proximity to resting potential), and myocyte electrical coupling via gap junctions
Sympathetic tone, vagal tone, plasma K+ concentration, and the density of IKr channels in the conduction system

SR Ca2+ release rate, crossbridge cycling speed, the rate of ventricular pressure development (dP/dt), and the resting membrane potential of upstream SA nodal pacemaker cells — none of which appear in the four-determinant table
questions.explanation:
The four major determinants of myocardial conduction velocity are: (1) current amplitude — the number of open Na+ or Ca2+ channels; (2) Vmax — the number and rate of channel opening during Phase 0 (Na+ gating is faster than Ca2+); (3) threshold — myocyte thresholds (−60 mV) are more hyperpolarized than nodal thresholds (−45 mV), aiding fast conduction in myocytes; (4) electrical coupling via gap junctions at intercalated discs.
Option A is incorrect: none of the four listed items (heart rate, AP duration, extracellular Ca2+, gap junction length) appear in the lecture’s determinants table.
Option C is incorrect: sympathetic/vagal tone and IKr density are modulators of heart rate and APD, not the four listed determinants.
Option D is incorrect: SR Ca2+ release, crossbridge cycling, and dP/dt are contractile (not conduction) variables; only resting membrane potential is adjacent to the determinants but is not one of the four listed.

questions.text: Lidocaine (a Class IB antiarrhythmic) is preferentially effective in treating arrhythmias in ischemic tissue compared with normal myocardium. Which property of Class IB drugs best explains this selectivity?
options: Class IB drugs bind exclusively to Na+ channels in the closed (resting) state; ischemia is proposed to increase the fraction of time channels spend in the closed state, thereby enhancing drug binding selectively in the ischemic zone compared with normal myocardium
Class IB drugs bind to both activated and inactivated Na+ channels with equal affinity; ischemic tissue has a higher absolute density of Na+ channels, so more drug can bind

Class IB drugs bind only to Na+ channels in the inactivated state; ischemia-induced membrane depolarization increases the fraction of channels held in the inactivated state, selectively enhancing binding in ischemic cells
Class IB drugs act by blocking delayed-rectifier K+ channels in ischemic tissue; K+ channel block lengthens the refractory period and suppresses ischemia-related arrhythmias
questions.explanation:
Class IB binds Na+ channels only in the inactivated state. Ischemia depolarizes the resting membrane potential (cells cannot repolarize fully due to ATP depletion), holding a larger fraction of Na+ channels in the inactivated state. This increases IB drug binding selectively in ischemic tissue while sparing normal cells that return fully to −90 mV.
Option A is incorrect: Class IB does not bind channels in the closed (resting) state; Class IA and IC bind in both activated and inactivated states.
Option B is incorrect: Class IA and IC (not IB) bind in both activated and inactivated states; furthermore, Na+ channel density does not increase with ischemia.
Option D is incorrect: Class IB targets Na+ channels, not K+ channels; K+ channel blockade is the mechanism of Class III drugs.

questions.text: Two Class I antiarrhythmics differ in when they bind Na+ channels and in their ECG signature. Flecainide (IC) persistently inhibits Na+ channels during diastole, while lidocaine (IB) inhibits them during systole. Which combination of ECG effects correctly matches these two drugs?
options: Flecainide: shortened QT interval, unchanged QRS width; Lidocaine: widened QRS complex, unchanged QT interval
Flecainide: widened QRS and prolonged QT interval; Lidocaine: unchanged QRS, shortened QT interval
Flecainide: unchanged QRS and unchanged QT interval; Lidocaine: widened QRS complex and prolonged QT interval
Flecainide: widened QRS complex, unchanged QT interval; Lidocaine: unchanged QRS width, shortened QT interval
questions.explanation:
Class IC (flecainide) persistently blocks Na+ channels during diastole, markedly slowing myocardial conduction (reduced Vmax) — this widens the QRS complex. Because ERP is unchanged, the QT interval does not lengthen. Class IB (lidocaine) blocks Na+ channels during systole, which shortens the action potential duration and reduces the QT interval, without significantly widening the QRS.
Option A is incorrect: the effects are reversed — flecainide widens QRS (not shortens QT) and lidocaine shortens QT (not widens QRS).
Option B is incorrect: flecainide does not prolong the QT interval; that is a Class III effect. Lidocaine does not widen QRS.
Option C is incorrect: flecainide has a significant QRS-widening effect (its hallmark ECG finding); unchanged QRS does not apply.

questions.text: A patient with persistent atrial fibrillation is prescribed a drug that blocks IKr and IKs K+ channels. Which combination of action potential changes and adverse cardiac effect is expected?
options: Blocked Phase 0 upstroke → reduced Vmax → widened QRS complex → risk of ventricular conduction block at rapid heart rates
Accelerated Phase 3 repolarization → shortened action potential duration → shortened QT interval → risk of symptomatic bradycardia due to excessive ERP shortening across the conduction system
Delayed Phase 3 repolarization → increased action potential duration and effective refractory period → prolonged QT interval → risk of torsades de pointes
Inhibited L-type Ca2+ channels during the plateau → shortened plateau → decreased contractility → risk of cardiogenic shock
questions.explanation:
Class III antiarrhythmics block K+ channels (IKr, IKs), delaying Phase 3 repolarization. This prolongs action potential duration and effective refractory period, which lengthens the QT interval on ECG. The prolonged QT interval predisposes to early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes (polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with twisting QRS morphology).
Option B is incorrect: K+ channel block delays (not accelerates) repolarization; QT is prolonged, not shortened.
Option A is incorrect: K+ channel block does not affect Phase 0 or Vmax; QRS widening from Na+ channel block is a Class I effect, not Class III.
Option D is incorrect: Ca2+ channel block is the mechanism of Class IV, not Class III; Class III acts on K+ channels.

questions.text: Sotalol is a Class III antiarrhythmic used for rate control and rhythm control in atrial fibrillation. Which ionic channel does it principally block, and what direct consequence does this have on Phase 3 of the ventricular action potential?
options: Sotalol blocks L-type Ca2+ channels (ICaL), shortening Phase 2 and reducing the plateau amplitude, which lowers the risk of early afterdepolarizations
Sotalol blocks fast Na+ channels in the inactivated state, slowing Phase 0 depolarization and widening the QRS complex without significantly changing the QT interval
Sotalol blocks the rapid delayed-rectifier K+ current (IKr), delaying Phase 3 repolarization and prolonging action potential duration and the QT interval
Sotalol opens background inward-rectifier K+ channels (IK1), hyperpolarizing the resting membrane potential and directly suppressing SA nodal automaticity
questions.explanation:
Sotalol is a Class III agent that blocks IKr (the rapid delayed-rectifier K+ current). Blocking IKr reduces the outward K+ current during Phase 3, prolonging the time needed for repolarization. This extends AP duration and QT interval, predisposing to torsades de pointes — the Class III adverse effect.
Option A is incorrect: sotalol does not block L-type Ca2+ channels; that is the mechanism of Class IV (diltiazem, verapamil).
Option B is incorrect: fast Na+ channel blockade defines Class I antiarrhythmics and produces QRS widening; sotalol is Class III acting on K+ channels.
Option D is incorrect: sotalol blocks (does not open) IKr; opening IK1 channels would hyperpolarize the cell, which is not the mechanism.

questions.text: A non-dihydropyridine L-type Ca2+ channel blocker (Class IV antiarrhythmic) is administered intravenously. Which combination of cardiac effects is expected?
options: Decreased contractility, decreased heart rate, decreased conduction velocity, and shortened action potential duration with shortened QT interval
Unchanged contractility, increased heart rate, decreased conduction velocity, and shortened PR interval
Decreased contractility, increased heart rate, unchanged conduction velocity, and shortened QRS complex
Increased contractility, decreased heart rate, increased conduction velocity, and prolonged QT interval — consistent with Ca2+ channel agonism, not the inhibition produced by Class IV agents
questions.explanation:
Class IV (e.g., diltiazem) blocks L-type Ca2+ channels during the plateau. This (1) reduces CICR from the SR — decreased contractility; (2) suppresses Ca2+-dependent automaticity in the SA node — decreased heart rate; (3) slows Ca2+-dependent conduction through the AV node — decreased conduction velocity; and (4) shortens the Ca2+-dependent plateau phase — shortened AP duration and QT interval.
Option D is incorrect: contractility decreases (not increases) and conduction velocity decreases (not increases) with L-type Ca2+ block.
Option B is incorrect: heart rate decreases (not increases) and contractility is impaired (not unchanged).
Option C is incorrect: conduction velocity decreases (not unchanged) because AV node conduction depends on L-type Ca2+ channels; QRS widening is not expected (that is a Class I effect).

questions.text: In severe hyperkalemia, the ECG characteristically shows a widened QRS complex. Which mechanistic sequence best explains this finding?
options: Elevated extracellular K+ makes EK less negative → resting membrane potential depolarizes → background K+ channels are constitutively open → excessive K+ efflux progressively slows Phase 3 repolarization → prolonged action potential duration appears as widened QRS

Elevated extracellular K+ makes EK less negative → resting membrane potential depolarizes toward EK → larger fraction of Na+ channels are held in the inactivated state → reduced Vmax of Phase 0 → slowed intraventricular conduction → widened QRS
Elevated extracellular K+ directly blocks L-type Ca2+ channels → shortened plateau → the QRS widens as a compensatory response to preserve diastolic filling time
Elevated extracellular K+ activates IKr channels → accelerated Phase 3 repolarization → shortened action potential → inadequate time for Na+ channel recovery from inactivation → widened QRS
questions.explanation:
When extracellular K+ rises, EK becomes less negative (the Nernst equation: raising [K+]o decreases the concentration gradient). The resting membrane potential follows EK upward (depolarizes). A chronically depolarized resting potential traps a larger fraction of voltage-gated Na+ channels in the inactivated state — they cannot close and reset. This reduces Vmax of Phase 0, slowing conduction through the ventricle, which manifests as QRS widening.
Option A is incorrect: K+ channel opening accelerates (not slows) repolarization; the QRS widens from slow Phase 0 conduction, not from slowed Phase 3 repolarization.
Option C is incorrect: hyperkalemia does not directly block L-type Ca2+ channels; QRS widening results from impaired Na+ channel availability, not from Ca2+ channel effects.
Option D is incorrect: IKr activation would shorten repolarization, which is not the mechanism of QRS widening; the mechanism is Na+ channel inactivation from a depolarized resting potential.

questions.text: Three Class I antiarrhythmic subclasses each affect Na+ channels but in distinct gating states, producing different effects on the effective refractory period (ERP). Which correctly matches quinidine (IA), lidocaine (IB), and flecainide (IC) to their expected ERP effects?
options: Quinidine (IA): decreased ERP; Lidocaine (IB): increased ERP; Flecainide (IC): unchanged ERP
Quinidine (IA): increased ERP; Lidocaine (IB): decreased ERP; Flecainide (IC): unchanged ERP
Quinidine (IA): unchanged ERP; Lidocaine (IB): decreased ERP; Flecainide (IC): increased ERP
Quinidine (IA): increased ERP; Lidocaine (IB): unchanged ERP; Flecainide (IC): decreased ERP
questions.explanation:
Class IA (quinidine) blocks Na+ channels in both activated and inactivated states and also blocks K+ channels, prolonging AP duration and therefore ERP. Class IB (lidocaine) blocks Na+ channels during systole, shortening AP duration and reducing ERP. Class IC (flecainide) blocks Na+ channels persistently during diastole, slowing conduction (widening QRS) without significantly changing AP duration or ERP.
Option A is incorrect: quinidine increases (not decreases) ERP, and lidocaine decreases (not increases) ERP.
Option C is incorrect: quinidine changes ERP significantly (increases it); its ERP effect is not unchanged.
Option D is incorrect: flecainide does not decrease ERP; its signature is QRS widening with unchanged ERP.
